economics.title: Salzburg Festival Ticket Queue
economics.context: Consider Salzburg festival-goers queuing overnight when discounted early-bird tickets sell out within minutes. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Minutes-long sell-outs at the posted price suggest quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
Overnight queues form when buyers expect shortage at the official price.
Persistent shortage forces resellers to cut prices below the sold-out official rate.
Adding extra performances shifts demand leftward because audiences dislike additional shows.
Raising the official ticket price increases shortage because fewer buyers withdraw.
tactical_explanations:
Early-bird tickets vanishing in minutes at the posted price means quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at that price. Sell-out speed is shortage evidence.

Buyers who still want the good at the low price compete with time, contacts, or willingness to pay more later. That pressure is exactly what pushes a competitive price upward.

Ceiling rules or sticky posted prices can freeze the shortage in place. Until the legal or listed price can move, quantity demanded stays above quantity supplied.

In Salzburg Festival Ticket Queue, that excess demand shows up as queues, waitlists, or vanishing stock at the posted ticket. Price has not yet risen enough to ration the scarce units or invite more supply.

So the statement is True.

Overnight queues form when buyers expect that official allocation will not cover everyone at the printed rate. Queuing is rationing by waiting under shortage expectations.

In Salzburg Festival Ticket Queue, that excess demand shows up as queues, waitlists, or vanishing stock at the posted ticket. Price has not yet risen enough to ration the scarce units or invite more supply.

Buyers who still want the good at the low price compete with time, contacts, or willingness to pay more later. That pressure is exactly what pushes a competitive price upward.

So the statement is True.

Persistent shortage at the official rate typically pushes resale prices above, not below, the sold-out face value. Resellers cut below official only if surplus pressure exists, which is not the festival queue story.

So the statement is False.

Extra performances expand supply of seats; they do not shift demand leftward because audiences dislike more shows. More supply eases shortage rather than reducing willingness to attend.

The because-clause overreaches. Even if one fragment sounds familiar, the causal link or always/never stretch does not hold.

Put the actors back in the correct category and the statement collapses without needing a new chapter of theory.

A concrete counterexample from Salzburg Festival Ticket Queue is enough: the absolute wording fails as soon as an ordinary case sits on the other side.

For letter D, keep Adding, extra, performances in the foreground; those words already decide whether the mechanism holds.

So the statement is False.

Raising the official ticket price lowers quantity demanded and can shrink shortage; it does not increase shortage by making fewer buyers withdraw. Withdrawal of marginal buyers is how higher prices ease excess demand.

If quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, the right label is surplus, not shortage. Empty-shelf stories do not fit a glut at the posted price.

Raising price usually eases shortage by cutting quantity demanded and inviting supply. Claiming the opposite reverses the adjustment logic.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Competition authority case
economics.context: Consider regulators investigate whether three mobile carriers colluded on text-message pricing nationally. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Investigating pricing across an entire national mobile market can involve macro-style market-wide analysis.
One subscriber choosing a cheaper text plan for her own phone is microeconomics.
Economics builds theories to explain firm behaviour and market outcomes including competition issues.
Microeconomics studies individual firm pricing strategies when one carrier alone is analysed.
Economics excludes market competition because only government budgets matter.
tactical_explanations:
A national probe into whether three mobile carriers colluded on text pricing looks across an entire industry market. That market-wide frame can borrow the language of broad, system-level analysis even though the product is still messaging rather than GDP. The letter's careful wording ("can involve macro-style market-wide analysis") fits that scale of inquiry.

So the statement is True.

A single subscriber switching to a cheaper text plan is a household-level choice inside one product market. That is ordinary microeconomics of consumer choice among plans.

The case also mentions a national collusion probe among operators, which is a different market-structure question. Treating the personal plan switch as if it answered the whole phone-market probe overreaches, so the letter does not stand as written.

So the statement is False.

Competition cases are standard territory for economic theory: how firms set prices, whether parallel pricing looks like collusion, and how market structure shapes outcomes. Building those explanations and predictions is what the discipline does.

Nothing in the mobile probe sits outside economics merely because regulators are involved. Firm behaviour and market outcomes, including competition issues, are core content rather than a side topic reserved for lawyers alone.

So the statement is True.

When the analyst isolates one carrier's pricing strategy on its own, the unit is a single firm. Microeconomics is the branch that studies that firm's incentives, costs, and prices without requiring a simultaneous model of national GDP.

So the statement is True.

Market competition is central to economics, not excluded from it. Government budgets matter in public finance, but they do not crowd firms, prices, and rivalry out of the subject. The absolute exclusion fails immediately.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: EU Services at Seventy-four Percent
economics.context: Consider a GDP report for an EU member state shows services at seventy-four percent of total output. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Service share alone does not prove every component of GDP is environmentally sustainable.
Seventy-four percent services indicates tertiary dominance rather than primary leadership.
Such a share is typical for economically advanced EU countries.
Seventy-four percent service share fits a highly developed EU economy pattern.
That pattern reflects rising relative importance of tertiary activity with development.
tactical_explanations:
A high service share says nothing by itself about environmental sustainability of every GDP component. Composition and green impact are separate questions.

So the statement is True.

Seventy-four percent services means the tertiary sector leads output, not the primary sector. Primary leadership would require extraction and farming to dominate the total.

So the statement is True.

Service shares around three-quarters of output are typical for economically advanced EU countries. The reported seventy-four percent therefore fits the developed-economy pattern rather than an emerging primary-heavy structure.

Students should read that percentage as a development marker in the three-sector story, not as proof that industry or farming disappeared. Relative tertiary weight is what the figure signals.

So the statement is True.

Seventy-four percent services aligns with a highly developed EU economy pattern in the chapter's stylised facts. It is the expected ballpark for advanced members.

So the statement is True.

Rising relative importance of tertiary activity with development is exactly what a seventy-four percent service share illustrates in the sector model.

So the statement is True.

economics.title: Micro balance sheet OR test
economics.context: Consider a design studio that reports eight staff, €2.4m turnover, and a €1.7m balance sheet. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A firm fails the medium test because both financial figures must be below their respective caps.
Medium enterprises employ fewer than two hundred and fifty people under EU definitions.
Because turnover is within €50m, balance sheet size is irrelevant for medium classification.
Two hundred and forty employees exceed the medium staff ceiling.
Thirty-eight staff alone keeps a firm in the small category despite turnover above €10m.
tactical_explanations:
Medium classification uses an OR on the financial side: turnover up to €50m or balance sheet up to €43m, plus fewer than 250 staff. Both financial figures need not sit under their caps at once.

A firm can miss one financial ceiling and still pass medium if the other financial measure and staff tests hold. Demanding both financial figures below their caps invents an AND rule the definition does not use.

So the statement is False.

EU medium enterprises employ fewer than two hundred and fifty people. That staff ceiling is the employment half of the medium size tests used with the financial caps.

So the statement is True.

Turnover within €50m does not make balance sheet size irrelevant. A balance sheet above €43m can still fail medium status when that route is the one being relied on and the other financial test also fails.

So the statement is False.

Two hundred and forty employees sit under the medium staff ceiling of fewer than 250. That headcount clears rather than exceeds the official limit.

So the statement is False.

Thirty-eight staff fit the small employee band, yet turnover above €10m can knock the firm out of small status. Staff alone cannot keep the small label once financial caps break.

So the statement is False.

economics.title: Voting Rights and Share Classes
economics.context: Analyze how common and preferred stock divide control and income rights among shareholders. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: At the annual stockholders' meeting, common stockholders ordinarily exercise voting rights on major resolutions.
Preferred shareholders always hold superior voting power over common shareholders at every meeting.
Preferred shares often trade voting rights for priority in dividend payments.
Investors may purchase shares partly to influence corporate decisions through those voting rights.
Dividend priority for preferred stock does not eliminate the discretionary nature of overall dividend policy.
tactical_explanations:
Common stockholders ordinarily cast votes at the annual meeting on major resolutions such as electing directors or approving structural changes. That voting role is the ordinary control channel attached to common equity, not a rare exception.

So the statement is True.

Preferred shares typically weaken or remove voting power in exchange for dividend priority. They do not always dominate common votes at every meeting. Treating preferred holders as perpetual vote superiors reverses the usual package: income preference often comes with less say, not more.

So the statement is False.

Preferred equity is frequently designed as a bargain: holders accept thinner voting rights and receive earlier claim on dividends when profits are distributed. Corporations sell that package to investors who want steadier income more than boardroom influence. Common stock keeps the primary AGM voice; preferred stock often sits closer to hybrid income paper. The trade is intentional, not accidental wording. When a firm needs capital without diluting control as sharply, preferred classes can raise money while voting remains concentrated among common shares. The statement correctly names that exchange of voice for dividend priority.

So the statement is True.

Buying shares can be partly about control. Voting rights let investors support or challenge board slates and major corporate acts, so some purchases are deliberate influence plays rather than pure portfolio bets.

So the statement is True.

Preferred dividend priority ranks claims when dividends are declared; it does not turn dividends into a legal certainty every year. Boards still decide whether and how much to distribute overall, so discretionary dividend policy survives the preferred preference rule.

So the statement is True.

economics.title: Internal and External Finance Classification
economics.context: Consider a manufacturing corporation that combines share capital from outside investors, retained profits, and a multi-year bank loan to expand production capacity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Equity finance encompasses both internal sources such as retained earnings and external sources such as share capital.
Short-term bank loans used to cover working capital are classified as short-term debt finance.
Debt finance is always external because borrowed funds create obligations to outside creditors.
The balance sheet reveals the sources of finance that a business has used in building its assets.
Large businesses are obliged to draw up a balance sheet showing how operations have been funded.
tactical_explanations:
Equity finance is not only new share issues from the market. Retained earnings supply internal equity while share capital supplies external equity under one equity heading.

So the statement is True.

Borrowing for a few months to bridge payroll or inventory is short-term debt finance. Working-capital loans of that kind do not become equity merely because production capacity expands afterward.

So the statement is True.

Borrowed money creates repayment obligations to creditors, so debt finance is treated as external in the overview. Even an owner loan is still debt owed outward from the entity's point of view when classed as credit. The manufacturing corporation's multi-year bank loan therefore sits with external debt beside share capital and retained profit. Internal equity and external equity remain separate from that borrowed slice.

So the statement is True.

Assets on one side of the balance sheet are funded by equity and liabilities on the other. Reading that statement of sources shows how the business has financed the plant and working capital it owns.

So the statement is True.

Large firms are required to present a balance sheet that discloses funding structure to readers. That obligation is why sources of finance appear in published statements rather than only in informal notes.

So the statement is True.

economics.title: Repair Reuse and Longer Product Life
economics.context: Consider an event-styling firm offering premium garment rental so clients avoid buying single-use outfits for occasional occasions. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Marketing responsibility includes recognising that promotional activity may encourage purchases beyond strict necessity.
Throwaway fashion is sustainable when garments are cheap because low price offsets short useful life.
Consumers who repair rather than replace functional goods reduce pressure on resources needed for new manufacturing.
Durable apparel that survives many seasons can circulate among several users before fibres are exhausted.
Budget plans are often exceeded when shoppers add non-essential items after exposure to targeted advertisements.
tactical_explanations:
Promotions can nudge people past planned baskets into impulse extras. Marketing teams that ignore that effect treat budgets as someone else's problem. Recognising the risk of unnecessary purchases is part of responsible promotional practice, exactly as the statement says.

So the statement is True.

Cheap throwaway fashion still burns materials, logistics, and landfill space after a few wears. A low shelf price does not cancel short useful life. Calling that pattern sustainable because garments are inexpensive confuses price with resource impact.

So the statement is False.

Fixing a working coat zipper or resoleing boots keeps fabric and hardware in use instead of sending the item to disposal. New manufacturing then faces less replacement demand for the same wardrobe function. Resource pressure falls when repair displaces fresh production runs. Consumers who choose that path reduce the materials and energy that would have gone into another unit. The statement links repair to lower manufacturing pressure correctly.

So the statement is True.

A well-made jacket that lasts several seasons can be worn by one person, then passed or rented to others before fibres fail. Circulation multiplies wear per unit of cloth. Durability is what makes that multi-user path realistic.

So the statement is True.

Targeted ads often surface non-essential add-ons after the planned items are chosen. Shoppers then overrun the budget they set before entering the store or site. That pattern matches everyday impulse overspend under promotion.

So the statement is True.

english.passage:
(1) In West Antarctica sits a glacier roughly the size of Great Britain, its ice cliffs facing an ocean now consistently warmer than at any point in recorded history. Thwaites Glacier holds enough ice that, were it to disintegrate entirely, global sea levels would rise by roughly 65 centimetres, a shift that would redraw coastlines from Bangladesh to Florida.

(2) What makes Thwaites especially alarming is not simply its size but its location. The glacier rests on bedrock that slopes downward inland, meaning that once retreat begins, warmer ocean water can flow ever deeper beneath the ice, accelerating melting rather than slowing it, a self-reinforcing process glaciologists call marine ice sheet instability.

(3) In 2019, researchers using ice-penetrating radar discovered a cavity beneath the glacier roughly twothirds the size of Manhattan, large enough to have once contained approximately 14 billion tonnes of ice that had already melted away. The cavity's existence confirmed that warm water was reaching, and eroding, the glacier's underside far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested.

(4) Thwaites does not melt in isolation. Acting as a natural buttress, its ice shelf currently holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland; researchers estimate that if this buttressing effect were entirely lost, surrounding glaciers could eventually contribute an additional three metres of sea-level rise, unfolding over centuries rather than years.

(5) Since the 1990s, satellite measurements show Thwaites has roughly doubled its rate of ice loss, though scientists caution that this acceleration has not proceeded smoothly; certain sections have periodically stabilised before resuming retreat, complicating efforts to extrapolate a single, simple future trajectory from past trends.

(6) The International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration, a joint venture funded by the United States and United Kingdom beginning in 2018, has coordinated dozens of research expeditions to the glacier, deploying underwater robots, autonomous sensors, and specially reinforced ships capable of navigating waters that had previously been considered too hazardous to survey directly.

(7) Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent. Some simulations suggest the glacier's most vulnerable sections could destabilise within several decades, while others project a substantially slower unfolding lasting multiple centuries, a divergence stemming partly from genuine scientific uncertainty and partly from the sheer difficulty of modelling ice behaviour deep beneath the ocean's surface.

(8) This uncertainty carries real consequences for coastal planning. Engineers designing sea walls, city planners rezoning flood-prone districts, and insurers pricing coastal property all require some estimate of future sea-level rise, yet current projections span a range wide enough to make precise, decades-ahead planning genuinely difficult.

(9) Whether Thwaites represents a slow-moving but ultimately containable hazard, or an early warning of instability capable of accelerating far faster than current models suggest, remains a question actively pursued by glaciologists studying the ice sheet's hidden underside.
english.passageTitle: The Doomsday Glacier — Racing to Predict a Silent Collapse

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Based on the passage, decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: Thwaites Glacier is roughly the size of Great Britain.
Full disintegration would raise sea levels by 65 centimetres.
Retreat slows once warm water reaches inland bedrock.
The glacier's bedrock slopes upward as it moves inland.
Marine ice sheet instability describes a self-reinforcing melting process.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Thwaites Glacier is roughly the size of Great Britain.**

Paragraph 1 opens with a direct size comparison: a glacier "roughly the size of Great Britain" sits in West Antarctica. The statement simply repeats that explicit scale, without adding numbers or geography the text never gives. Do not confuse this Britain-scale analogy with the later Manhattan cavity or the 65-centimetre sea-level figure—those are separate measurements. The wording "roughly the size of Great Britain" is the exact anchor you need for a bare size claim.

**Tip:** Treat bare size or place analogies as true when they echo the passage word-for-word or with a light paraphrase.

The size match is stated outright in Paragraph 1, so the claim is true.

**B) Full disintegration would raise sea levels by 65 centimetres.**

Still in Paragraph 1, the text says that if Thwaites were to "disintegrate entirely, global sea levels would rise by roughly 65 centimetres." The statement's "full disintegration" is just a clean rephrase of that total-collapse scenario, and the centimetre figure is unchanged. Watch that you do not swap this 65 cm Thwaites-only figure for Paragraph 4's additional three metres from surrounding glaciers. The phrase "disintegrate entirely" plus "roughly 65 centimetres" is the precise pairing the statement restates.

The 65-centimetre rise is the passage's own number for complete loss, so the claim matches.

**C) Retreat slows once warm water reaches inland bedrock.**

Paragraph 2 says the opposite: once retreat begins, warmer water can flow ever deeper beneath the ice, "accelerating melting rather than slowing it." The statement flips that causal direction—from acceleration to slowing—so it fails against the stability mechanism the text names. The trap is the verb "slows": the passage insists the feedback speeds melt, not brakes it. Match the claim against the exact contrast "accelerating melting rather than slowing it" and the reverse becomes obvious.

**Trap:** Watch for verbs that reverse the marine ice-sheet feedback; the passage insists melt speeds up, not cools down.

The claim reverses Paragraph 2's accelerating feedback, so it fails.

**D) The glacier's bedrock slopes upward as it moves inland.**

Paragraph 2 locates the danger in bedrock that "slopes downward inland," not upward. An upward slope would block warm-water intrusion; a downward one enables the self-reinforcing retreat the paragraph describes. The statement simply swaps the slope direction. "Upward" is a one-word antonym trap of "downward inland," so any slope claim must keep that direction intact. The passage's wording "slopes downward inland" is the fact that kills this rewrite.

Downward inland, not upward, is the bedrock fact, so the claim is false.

**E) Marine ice sheet instability describes a self-reinforcing melting process.**

Paragraph 2 ends by labelling that self-reinforcing melt loop: "a self-reinforcing process glaciologists call marine ice sheet instability." The statement faithfully restates that definition—name and mechanism line up. Nothing in the label invents a different process or a different technical name. The clause that equates "self-reinforcing process" with "marine ice sheet instability" is the definitional match the statement copies.

The term and the feedback process are equated in Paragraph 2, so the claim is true.

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Based on the passage, decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: The 2019 cavity was roughly two-thirds Manhattan's size.
The cavity once held about 14 billion tonnes of ice.
Surface observations alone had already revealed this cavity's full extent.
Losing the ice shelf's buttress could add three metres of sea-level rise.
That additional rise would unfold within a single decade.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The 2019 cavity was roughly two-thirds Manhattan's size.**

Paragraph 3 reports that in 2019 radar found a cavity "roughly twothirds the size of Manhattan." The statement's hyphenated "two-thirds" is the same fraction; it does not invent a larger or later cavity. Spelling or hyphenation differences ("two-thirds" vs "twothirds") do not change the fraction the passage gives. Anchor on "roughly twothirds the size of Manhattan" as the cavity's stated scale.

The Manhattan-scale comparison is Paragraph 3's own measure, so the claim is true.

**B) The cavity once held about 14 billion tonnes of ice.**

The same sentence says the cavity was "large enough to have once contained approximately 14 billion tonnes of ice that had already melted away." "About" fairly covers "approximately," and the tonne count is unchanged. Softeners like "about" and "approximately" are interchangeable paraphrases, not new quantities. The figure "approximately 14 billion tonnes of ice" is the exact number the statement echoes.

The 14-billion-tonne figure is stated in Paragraph 3, so the claim matches.

**C) Surface observations alone had already revealed this cavity's full extent.**

Paragraph 3 stresses the opposite: warm-water erosion was "far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested." Radar, not surface surveys, revealed the cavity's scale. The statement credits surface data with a discovery the text withholds from them. The word "already" falsely pretends surface methods had finished the job before radar. Compare the claim with "far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested" and the understatement becomes clear.

**Trap:** "Already" + surface methods is a common flip—Paragraph 3 says surface data understated the problem.

Surface observations alone missed this extent, so the claim fails.

**D) Losing the ice shelf's buttress could add three metres of sea-level rise.**

Paragraph 4 estimates that if the buttressing effect were entirely lost, surrounding glaciers "could eventually contribute an additional three metres of sea-level rise." The statement correctly ties that three-metre add-on to loss of the ice shelf's buttress role. Do not confuse this additional three metres with Paragraph 1's roughly 65 centimetres for Thwaites alone. The wording "additional three metres of sea-level rise" after lost buttressing is the exact estimate restated here.

The three-metre estimate is Paragraph 4's figure for lost buttressing, so the claim is true.

**E) That additional rise would unfold within a single decade.**

Paragraph 4 immediately times the extra rise as "unfolding over centuries rather than years." A single decade is far shorter than that multi-century window, so the statement invents a rapid timetable the text rejects. "Years" already rules out a decade-scale sprint; "centuries" stretches the window even further. Match any timing claim against "unfolding over centuries rather than years" before accepting a fast calendar.

Centuries, not a decade, is the span given, so the claim is false.

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Based on the passage, decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: Since the 1990s, ice loss has roughly doubled.
This acceleration has proceeded smoothly without any pauses.
The joint research collaboration began in 2018.
All model projections agree closely on collapse timing.
Coastal planners currently face a genuinely wide projection range.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since the 1990s, ice loss has roughly doubled.**

Paragraph 5 reports that satellite measurements show Thwaites "has roughly doubled its rate of ice loss" since the 1990s. The statement repeats that doubling without inventing a steeper surge or a different start year. "Roughly doubled" is already a softener, so do not treat the claim as demanding an exact 2.00 multiplier. The phrase "roughly doubled its rate of ice loss" since the 1990s is the statistic the statement copies.

The doubled-loss claim is Paragraph 5's own statistic, so it is true.

**B) This acceleration has proceeded smoothly without any pauses.**

The same paragraph cautions that acceleration "has not proceeded smoothly"; sections have "periodically stabilised before resuming retreat." "Without any pauses" erases those temporary stabilisations the text explicitly records. Overall doubling and stop-start local behaviour can both be true; the trap is treating them as mutually exclusive. The wording "has not proceeded smoothly" plus periodic stabilisation directly kills a no-pause claim.

**Trap:** Doubling overall does not mean a smooth, unbroken climb—Paragraph 5 flags stop-start behaviour.

Pauses and restabilisations contradict "smoothly," so the claim fails.

**C) The joint research collaboration began in 2018.**

Paragraph 6 introduces the International Thwaites Glacier Collaboration as a U.S.–U.K. venture "beginning in 2018." The statement names that start date accurately and invents no earlier founding year. A founding year is not a claim that all scientific uncertainty ended that year—later paragraphs still show divergent models. The exact anchor is "beginning in 2018" for the joint U.S.–U.K. collaboration.

The 2018 start is stated in Paragraph 6, so the claim is true.

**D) All model projections agree closely on collapse timing.**

Paragraph 7 opens with projections that "remain strikingly divergent"—decades in some runs, centuries in others. "Agree closely" is the exact opposite of that advertised mismatch. "All" plus "agree closely" is a unanimity rewrite the paragraph never supports. The opening line "Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent" is enough to reject close agreement.

Striking divergence overturns close agreement, so the claim is false.

**E) Coastal planners currently face a genuinely wide projection range.**

Paragraph 8 says current projections "span a range wide enough to make precise, decades-ahead planning genuinely difficult." Coastal engineers, planners, and insurers all work under that spread. The statement's "genuinely wide" tracks the passage's own wording. The difficulty is about the width of the range, not about planners ignoring sea-level risk altogether. Echo "span a range wide enough" and "genuinely difficult" when checking this synthesis of planning trouble.

The wide projection span for coastal planning is Paragraph 8's point, so the claim matches.

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Based on the passage, decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: Downward-sloping bedrock helps explain accelerating, self-reinforcing retreat.
If loss doubled since the 1990s, retreat has clearly worsened.
Divergent models imply scientists fully agree on collapse timing.
Buttressing loss implies inland glaciers depend partly on Thwaites.
Stabilised sections prove the glacier's overall retreat has ended.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Downward-sloping bedrock helps explain accelerating, self-reinforcing retreat.**

Paragraph 2 links bedrock that "slopes downward inland" to ever-deeper warm water and "accelerating melting," which glaciologists call "marine ice sheet instability." The inference is not a stretch: the slope is offered as the mechanism behind the self-reinforcing speed-up. "Helps explain" only asks for a causal link the paragraph already draws, not for a claim that slope is the sole cause of all ice loss. Re-read "slopes downward inland, meaning that… accelerating melting" as the mechanism chain the inference restates.

The bedrock geometry and the feedback are tied together in Paragraph 2, so the inference holds.

**B) If loss doubled since the 1990s, retreat has clearly worsened.**

Paragraph 5's doubling of the ice-loss rate since the 1990s is already framed as acceleration (even with intermittent pauses). A higher loss rate is a straightforward worsening of retreat intensity relative to that earlier baseline. Temporary local stabilisations do not cancel the overall rate increase the satellites show. "Clearly worsened" here means a worse ice-loss rate than the 1990s baseline, which "roughly doubled" supports.

**Tip:** "Clearly worsened" here tracks rate of ice loss, not a claim that every section is always retreating at once.

Doubled loss since the 1990s supports a worse retreat rate, so the inference is true.

**C) Divergent models imply scientists fully agree on collapse timing.**

Paragraph 7 calls the projections "strikingly divergent" and traces that gap to uncertainty and hard-to-model ice physics. Divergence is evidence of disagreement about timing, not of "full agree[ment]." The inference flips the logical force of the word. "Imply…fully agree" is an illicit leap from disagreement-language to unanimity. Keep "strikingly divergent" as proof that timing consensus is missing, not present.

**Trap:** "Divergent" never licenses unanimous timing; it blocks it.

Divergence contradicts full agreement, so the claim fails.

**D) Buttressing loss implies inland glaciers depend partly on Thwaites.**

Paragraph 4 says Thwaites' ice shelf "holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland," and that losing that buttress could unlock metres of extra rise from surrounding glaciers. Dependence of inland ice on Thwaites' buttress is exactly what that relationship implies. "Partly" is the safe hedge: the shelf holds ice back, so inland mass is not wholly independent of Thwaites. The phrase "holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland" is the dependence clue the inference uses.

The inland buttressing role supports partial dependence, so the inference is true.

**E) Stabilised sections prove the glacier's overall retreat has ended.**

Paragraph 5 notes only that certain sections "periodically stabilised before resuming retreat." Temporary pauses before restarting do not prove that overall retreat has ended; they complicate a simple future path while retreat continues. "Prove…has ended" overclaims from local, temporary pauses to a finished glacier-wide story. The sequence "stabilised before resuming retreat" shows pauses are interruptions, not an ending.

Stabilisation then "resuming retreat" overturns an "ended" verdict, so the claim is false.

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Based on the passage, decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: The 2019 cavity discovery helps explain the doubled loss rate since the 1990s.
Uncertain projections help explain why coastal planning remains genuinely difficult.
Because collaboration began in 2018, all uncertainty was fully resolved by then.
Buttressing loss and the three-metre estimate both concern ice beyond Thwaites itself.
Bedrock sloping downward is unrelated to the described instability process.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The 2019 cavity discovery helps explain the doubled loss rate since the 1990s.**

Paragraph 3's cavity shows warm water eroding the underside far more than surface clues suggested; Paragraph 5 records roughly doubled ice loss since the 1990s. Linking underside melt revealed in 2019 to that accelerated loss is a fair cross-section synthesis the text invites, even without a single sentence that pairs the two facts. "Helps explain" only needs a supporting mechanism, not a claim that the cavity is the sole cause of every tonne lost. Join basal erosion "far more extensively than surface observations alone had suggested" with the doubled-loss trend as the synthesis the item tests.

**Tip:** Synthesis items can join mechanism (basal melt) to trend (doubled loss) when both are in the passage.

Basal erosion and doubled loss fit together, so the synthesis holds.

**B) Uncertain projections help explain why coastal planning remains genuinely difficult.**

Paragraph 7–8 supply the causal chain: strikingly divergent models create wide projection ranges, and Paragraph 8 says that spread makes "precise, decades-ahead planning genuinely difficult" for coastal work. The statement restates the passage's own bridge from uncertainty to planning trouble. The difficulty is attributed to the width of the range, not to a claim that no planning is possible at all. Trace "strikingly divergent" models into the "range wide enough" that makes planning "genuinely difficult."

Wide, uncertain projections are Paragraph 8's reason for planning difficulty, so the claim is true.

**C) Because collaboration began in 2018, all uncertainty was fully resolved by then.**

Paragraph 6 dates the collaboration to 2018; Paragraphs 7–9 still present divergent models and an open question about Thwaites' hazard. Launching research does not mean uncertainty vanished that year—the later paragraphs prove it remains. "Because…fully resolved" invents a causal finish line the founding date never supplies. Keep "beginning in 2018" as a start date and "strikingly divergent" projections as proof the unknowns continue.

**Trap:** A start date is not a resolution date; later paragraphs keep the unknowns alive.

Ongoing divergent projections overturn "fully resolved by 2018," so the claim fails.

**D) Buttressing loss and the three-metre estimate both concern ice beyond Thwaites itself.**

Paragraph 4's buttress holds back "a much larger mass of ice further inland," and the three metres come from "surrounding glaciers" if that effect is lost. Both details point past Thwaites' own ice to the inland system it pins in place. The synthesis is about whose ice supplies the extra rise, not about whether Thwaites itself also melts. "Further inland" and "surrounding glaciers" are the beyond-Thwaites cues both halves of the claim share.

Inland ice and surrounding glaciers are beyond Thwaites alone, so the synthesis is true.

**E) Bedrock sloping downward is unrelated to the described instability process.**

Paragraph 2 presents downward-sloping bedrock as the setup that lets warm water deepen the retreat and feed "marine ice sheet instability." Calling the slope "unrelated" severs the mechanism the paragraph exists to explain. "Unrelated" is a disconnect trap: the text uses "meaning that" to weld slope geometry to the named instability. Re-read the full chain from "slopes downward inland" through accelerating melt to "marine ice sheet instability."

The slope is the instability's geometric cause, so the claim is false.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Based on the passage, decide whether each given meaning matches the word's actual use.
statements: In Paragraph 2, "self-reinforcing" means weakening over repeated cycles.
In Paragraph 3, "eroding" means gradually wearing something away.
In Paragraph 4, "buttress" means something that supports and holds back.
In Paragraph 6, "hazardous" means completely safe and risk-free.
In Paragraph 9, "hidden" means fully visible and easily observed.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In Paragraph 2, "self-reinforcing" means weakening over repeated cycles.**

In Paragraph 2 the process accelerates melt rather than slowing it—the loop strengthens itself. "Weakening over repeated cycles" is the opposite polarity of a self-reinforcing feedback. Context already pairs the label with accelerating melt, so a fade-out gloss cannot fit. Read "self-reinforcing process" next to "accelerating melting rather than slowing it" before accepting any antonym.

**Trap:** "Self-" compounds often tempt antonym glosses; here the ice-sheet loop intensifies, it does not fade.

Accelerating, not weakening, is the sense in Paragraph 2, so the gloss fails.

**B) In Paragraph 3, "eroding" means gradually wearing something away.**

Paragraph 3 says warm water was "reaching, and eroding, the glacier's underside"—progressive basal wear. "Gradually wearing something away" is exactly that geologic sense. Nothing in the sentence turns eroding into a sudden, one-time snap. The paired verbs "reaching, and eroding" describe ongoing underside damage by warm water.

Gradual wear matches how Paragraph 3 uses "eroding," so the meaning holds.

**C) In Paragraph 4, "buttress" means something that supports and holds back.**

Paragraph 4 calls the ice shelf a "natural buttress" that "holds back a much larger mass of ice further inland." Support-plus-restraint is the role the sentence assigns. The gloss does not invent a decorative or unrelated sense of the word. "Natural buttress" plus "holds back" is the contextual definition the statement restates.

Holding inland ice back is the buttress function named there, so the gloss is true.

**D) In Paragraph 6, "hazardous" means completely safe and risk-free.**

Paragraph 6 describes waters once "considered too hazardous to survey directly"—dangerous enough to avoid. "Completely safe and risk-free" is the antonym of that risk label. "Too hazardous to survey" only makes sense if the waters were risky, not safe. Keep hazardous as a danger word tied to waters that needed special ships and robots.

Hazardous marks danger, not safety, so the claimed meaning fails.

**E) In Paragraph 9, "hidden" means fully visible and easily observed.**

Paragraph 9 closes on the ice sheet's "hidden underside"—material researchers still pursue because it is not in plain view. "Fully visible" reverses that sense. If the underside were easily observed, glaciologists would not still be chasing that open question. "Hidden underside" signals concealment, the opposite of fully visible.

Hidden means concealed, not visible, so the gloss is false.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Based on the passage, decide whether each given meaning matches the word's actual use.
statements: In Paragraph 1, "disintegrate" means to break apart completely.
In Paragraph 5, "extrapolate" means to project forward from existing trends.
In Paragraph 7, "divergent" means closely matching one another.
In Paragraph 8, "genuinely" means falsely or only apparently.
In Paragraph 2, "accelerating" means slowing down gradually.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In Paragraph 1, "disintegrate" means to break apart completely.**

Paragraph 1 weighs what happens if Thwaites were to "disintegrate entirely"—total breakup releasing enough ice for a ~65 cm rise. "Break apart completely" tracks that total-collapse sense. The adverb "entirely" already pushes the verb toward total breakup, not a minor chip. Match "disintegrate entirely" with complete breaking apart as the contextual gloss.

Entire breakup is how Paragraph 1 uses the verb, so the meaning holds.

**B) In Paragraph 5, "extrapolate" means to project forward from existing trends.**

Paragraph 5 says stop-start retreat complicates efforts "to extrapolate a single, simple future trajectory from past trends." That is textbook projecting-forward from known data. The from-phrase "from past trends" is the clue that extrapolation starts with existing evidence. Keep that forward-projection sense rather than inventing a meaning like "ignore past data."

Projecting a future path from past trends is exactly the Paragraph 5 sense, so the gloss is true.

**C) In Paragraph 7, "divergent" means closely matching one another.**

Paragraph 7's projections "remain strikingly divergent," with some runs on decades and others on centuries. "Closely matching" erases that split. Decades-versus-centuries timelines are concrete proof of separation, not alignment. Reject any synonym that turns "strikingly divergent" into agreement.

**Trap:** Do not gloss divergent as "aligned"; the paragraph's decades-versus-centuries contrast proves separation.

Divergent means differing, not matching, so the claim fails.

**D) In Paragraph 8, "genuinely" means falsely or only apparently.**

Paragraph 8 says planning is "genuinely difficult" because the projection range is wide—"genuinely" intensifies real difficulty, not fake or apparent difficulty. "Falsely" is an antonym gloss that would cancel the adverb's intensifying job. Read "genuinely difficult" as truly hard planning under a wide projection span.

Genuinely means truly, not falsely, so the gloss is false.

**E) In Paragraph 2, "accelerating" means slowing down gradually.**

Paragraph 2 says warmer water leads to "accelerating melting rather than slowing it." The text even pairs accelerating against slowing, so "slowing down gradually" is the denied opposite. When a sentence says X rather than Y, Y cannot be the meaning of X. Use "accelerating melting rather than slowing it" as the built-in antonym test.

Accelerating is speeding melt, not slowing it, so the meaning fails.

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: "Had retreat not accelerated, sea levels would have risen slower."
"Scientists recommended that the team monitors the cavity closely."
"The number of research expeditions continue to grow yearly."
"Neither the sensors nor the ship were fully reliable."
"Having mapped the cavity, researchers revised their models."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had retreat not accelerated, sea levels would have risen slower."**

This is a third-conditional counterfactual with inverted Had + past participle ("Had retreat not accelerated") paired with "would have risen." The comparative adverb "slower" is acceptable exam English beside "more slowly" when comparing rates. The structure is equivalent to "If retreat had not accelerated, sea levels would have risen slower," just with fronted Had. Keep the pairing Had + past participle in the if-clause substitute and would have + past participle in the result.

**Tip:** Inversion (Had + subject + past participle) is just another way to write If + past perfect.

The inverted third conditional is well formed, so the sentence stands.

**B) "Scientists recommended that the team monitors the cavity closely."**

After recommend + that, exam English wants the mandative subjunctive: base form monitor, not third-person monitors. The finite "monitors" treats the clause like an ordinary present indicative. Singular "team" tempts people into -s agreement, but the subjunctive still drops the -s. Fix the line by restoring the base verb after recommend that.

**Trap:** Recommend/insist/require + that → base verb, even with a singular subject.

The subjunctive needs "monitor," so this wording fails — "Scientists recommended that the team monitor the cavity closely."

**C) "The number of research expeditions continue to grow yearly."**

The head of the subject is "number," which is singular, so the verb should be continues. "Continue" wrongly agrees with the plural noun inside the of-phrase ("expeditions"). Ignore the nearest plural noun when the head is "the number of." Swap continue for continues to match singular number.

**Tip:** The number of → singular; a number of → plural.

Singular "number" needs "continues," so the line fails — "The number of research expeditions continues to grow yearly."

**D) "Neither the sensors nor the ship were fully reliable."**

Neither…nor joins a plural noun ("sensors") and a singular one ("ship"). In this bank's mixed-number reading, plural agreement is allowed because one member of the pair is plural, so "were" can stand. Do not force nearest-noun singular "was" when the bank treats a plural partner as licensing plural agreement. Here "sensors" in the neither…nor pair is what keeps "were" acceptable.

**Tip:** When neither…nor mixes numbers, check which agreement rule the item expects—here the plural partner licenses "were."

With a plural noun in the neither…nor pair, "were" fits, so the sentence is sound.

**E) "Having mapped the cavity, researchers revised their models."**

The perfect participle "Having mapped" correctly sets mapping as earlier work by the same agents who then "revised"—researchers are both the mappers and the revisers, so there is no dangling modifier. Perfect participial openers mark prior action by the subject that follows, which is exactly this pattern. Confirm that "researchers" is the only logical subject of both "Having mapped" and "revised."

The participial opener attaches cleanly to "researchers," so the wording holds.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: "No sooner had radar scanned the ice than the cavity appeared."
"The programme, along with related studies, were funded jointly."
"Each of the models have projected differing timelines."
"By the time data arrives, projections will have already shifted."
"The readings, which were gathered yearly, show accelerating melt."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had radar scanned the ice than the cavity appeared."**

No sooner + inverted past perfect ("had radar scanned") pairs with than + past simple ("appeared"). That is the classic No sooner…than pattern for a near-immediate follow-on event. Do not replace than with when, and keep the Had-inversion after No sooner. The finished scan (past perfect) before the appearance (past simple) is the time order the idiom encodes.

The inversion and than-clause are correctly built, so the sentence stands.

**B) "The programme, along with related studies, were funded jointly."**

The real subject is singular "programme"; the parenthetical "along with related studies" does not make the verb plural. Were should be was. Comma-wrapped add-ons after the head never rewrite subject–verb number. Restore singular agreement: was funded jointly.

**Trap:** Along with / as well as / together with never turns a singular head into a plural subject.

Singular "programme" needs "was funded," so this fails — "The programme, along with related studies, was funded jointly."

**C) "Each of the models have projected differing timelines."**

Each of + plural noun still takes a singular verb: has projected, not have. "Each" points one-by-one and keeps the head singular. The plural "models" after of is a distractor, not the agreement controller. Change have to has to satisfy Each.

"Each" demands singular "has," so the line fails — "Each of the models has projected differing timelines."

**D) "By the time data arrives, projections will have already shifted."**

"By the time" + present ("arrives") sets a future reference point; "will have already shifted" places that change before data arrives—future perfect for prior completion. Present arrives is the usual tense after by the time when the main clause is future-oriented. Future perfect marks the shift as finished before that arrival moment.

Completion before a future "by the time" moment is exactly future perfect's job, so the wording is sound.

**E) "The readings, which were gathered yearly, show accelerating melt."**

Plural "readings" correctly takes "were" in the non-restrictive relative clause and "show" in the main clause. Number agreement is consistent throughout. The commas mark a non-restrictive which-clause, but that does not change plural agreement. Keep both were and show plural to match readings.

Plural subject and plural verbs align, so the sentence holds.

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Consider this sentence from the passage: "Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent." Decide whether each paraphrase preserves its meaning.
statements: Forecasts for the glacier's future differ sharply from one another.
Forecasts for the glacier's future agree closely with each other.
The glacier's future is no longer being modelled at all.
Predictions about the glacier's fate vary considerably between models.
Every model now predicts the exact same outcome confidently.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Forecasts for the glacier's future differ sharply from one another.**

The original line is "Model projections of Thwaites' future remain strikingly divergent." "Forecasts…differ sharply" preserves both the modelling topic and the strong-disagreement sense of "strikingly divergent." "Differ sharply" is a fair upgrade of "divergent" without inventing agreement or abandoned modelling. Keep the same subject (future forecasts/projections) and the same clash among them.

Sharp difference between forecasts is a faithful paraphrase, so the line matches.

**B) Forecasts for the glacier's future agree closely with each other.**

"Agree closely" is the antonym of "strikingly divergent." The paraphrase reverses the original's core claim about model disagreement. Synonym checks fail when the rewrite flips polarity while keeping the topic. Any close-agreement version of "strikingly divergent" must be rejected.

**Trap:** Synonym traps often flip divergent ↔ agree; reject any close-agreement rewrite.

Close agreement contradicts divergence, so this paraphrase fails.

**C) The glacier's future is no longer being modelled at all.**

The original asserts that model projections still exist and disagree; it never says modelling has stopped. "No longer being modelled" invents a cessation the sentence does not contain. Divergent projections presuppose active modelling, so a stop-modelling rewrite cannot be faithful. Stay inside "Model projections…remain strikingly divergent"—existence plus disagreement, not abandonment.

Abandoned modelling is not in the original, so the paraphrase fails.

**D) Predictions about the glacier's fate vary considerably between models.**

"Vary considerably between models" restates divergent projections without softening or reversing them. "Fate" and "predictions" stay within the same forecasting domain as "model projections…future." Considerable variation is the same strong-difference idea as "strikingly divergent," just in different words. Accept paraphrases that keep between-model disagreement intact.

Considerable between-model variation keeps the original meaning, so the paraphrase holds.

**E) Every model now predicts the exact same outcome confidently.**

Unanimous, confident sameness cancels "strikingly divergent." The paraphrase invents agreement and certainty the source line denies. "Every…exact same…confidently" stacks three overclaims the original never supports. Match the rewrite against "remain strikingly divergent" and the polarity flip is immediate.

Identical confident outcomes reverse the original, so this paraphrase is false.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Notwithstanding the delayed train, the friends still made the exhibition opening — and despite the same delay, they refused to skip the café stop.
Despite delayed trains, they reached the gallery; however, several rooms had already closed for cleaning.
Although delayed trains, they reached the gallery, however several rooms had already closed for cleaning.
Owing to the delayed train, they walked the last kilometre along the canal.
Because of delayed trains were overcrowded, they walked the last kilometre along the canal.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Notwithstanding the delayed train, the friends still made the exhibition opening — and despite the same delay, they refused to skip the café stop.**

Despite + "the same delay" in the second half is correctly formed as a noun concession, and the sentence stays grammatical. Friends still making the opening and refusing to skip the café both fit the contrast story. When two contrast tools appear, check each chunk separately — this despite use is fine.

Despite + "the same delay" in the second chunk is a clean noun concession, so the sentence is **true**.
**B) Despite delayed trains, they reached the gallery; however, several rooms had already closed for cleaning.**

Despite + "delayed trains" and semicolon + however are both well formed. Stacking two contrast tools is fine if each obeys its own rule: noun after despite, strong punctuation before however. They reach the gallery; several rooms have already closed.

Despite + delayed trains and semicolon + however each obey their own rules, so the wording is **true**.
**C) Although delayed trains, they reached the gallery, however several rooms had already closed for cleaning.**

Although lacks a clause ("Although delayed trains"), and however is joined with only a weak comma. Two linker errors can hide in one sentence — check each separately. Either fault alone would already force **false**.

**Trap:** Dense double-linker fails are hard because one error can mask the other.

Although lacks a clause and however sits after only a weak comma, so this is **false** — "Although trains were delayed, they reached the gallery; however, several rooms had already closed for cleaning."
**D) Owing to the delayed train, they walked the last kilometre along the canal.**

Owing to + "the delayed train" correctly states the reason for walking the last kilometre. Travel delays often pair with owing to in formal notices. The noun cause matches the linker.

Owing to + "the delayed train" names the canal-walk cause cleanly, so the line is **true**.
**E) Because of delayed trains were overcrowded, they walked the last kilometre along the canal.**

Because of + finite clause is illegal. "Because of delayed trains were overcrowded" → "Because delayed trains were overcrowded" or "Because of overcrowded delayed trains." If a verb like were sits after because of, rewrite immediately.

**Trap:** Because of + were is the classic hybrid trap buried in a longer travel sentence.

Because of cannot stack onto a finite were-overcrowded clause, so the wording is **false** — "Because delayed trains were overcrowded, they walked the last kilometre along the canal."

math.title: Assigning Paper Reviewers
math.context:
Five researchers - Petra, Quinn, Ravi, Sana, and Theo - are being assigned to review a paper. The assignment follows these rules:

1. If Petra reviews, then Quinn does not review.

2. Ravi reviews unless Sana reviews.

3. If Quinn does not review, then Theo reviews.

4. At least one of Petra or Sana reviews.

5. If Theo reviews, then Ravi does not review.

6. Sana reviews only if Petra reviews.
statements: Petra must review the paper in every valid assignment.
If Quinn reviews, then Petra does not review.
It is possible for Ravi to review the paper in some valid assignment.
In the (unique) valid assignment, both Theo and Sana review the paper.
There are multiple different valid ways to assign reviewers consistent with all six rules.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The claim says Petra reviews in every valid assignment. Test the opposite by assuming $\neg P$. Rule (6) is $S\Rightarrow P$, so its contrapositive gives

$$\neg P\overset{\text{contrapose of }(6)}{\Rightarrow}\neg S.$$

Rule (4) requires at least one of Petra or Sana:

$$(4)$$

$$P\lor S.$$

Under the assumption, both disjuncts are false. Thus Petra's absence makes rule (4) impossible to satisfy, so Petra is forced to review.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The claim asks what follows if Quinn reviews. Rule (1) says

$$(1)$$

$$P\Rightarrow\neg Q.$$

Taking the contrapositive reverses and negates both sides:

$$\neg(\neg Q)\Rightarrow\neg P,$$

so

$$Q\Rightarrow\neg P.$$

Therefore Quinn's presence forces Petra's absence, exactly as claimed.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The claim needs at least one valid assignment with Ravi. Petra is already forced in by rule (4) together with rule (6). Rule (1) then forces Quinn out, and rule (3) forces Theo in:

$$P\overset{(1)}{\Rightarrow}\neg Q \overset{(3)}{\Rightarrow}T.$$

Rule (5) now applies:

$$T\overset{(5)}{\Rightarrow}\neg R.$$

Thus every valid assignment forces Ravi out. Assuming Ravi in would collide with the forced $\neg R$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The claim says the unique assignment includes both Theo and Sana. Begin with Petra, who is forced in. Rules (1) and (3) then force Quinn out and Theo in:

$$P\overset{(1)}{\Rightarrow}\neg Q \overset{(3)}{\Rightarrow}T.$$

Rule (5) forces Ravi out. Rule (2) requires $R\lor S$, so Ravi's absence forces Sana in:

$$

math.title: Flow Rate Regulation in Coolant Networks
math.context:
A chemical production facility operates a closed-loop coolant network where volumetric flow rates are regulated by setting an operational parameter $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Fluid dynamicists model different sections of this piping network using five specialized rate-of-flow equations:

1. The main return line equation:
$$\frac{2x}{x-1} - \frac{3}{x+2} = \frac{6}{x^2+x-2} + 1$$

2. The alternative bypass line equation:
$$\frac{x}{x-3} - \frac{2}{x+3} = \frac{18}{x^2-9} + 1$$

3. The pressurized suction line equation:
$$\sqrt{2x+7} - x = 2$$

4. The directional regulator valve equation:
$$|3x - 2| = 2x - 5$$

5. The harmonic booster pump cycle equation:
$$(x^2 - 2x)^2 - 11(x^2 - 2x) + 24 = 0$$
statements: Clearing denominators in the main return line equation yields the quadratic relation $x^2 - 1 = 0$, but the candidate $x = 1$ is an extraneous root excluded by the domain restriction $x \notin \{-2, 1\}$, leaving $x = -1$ as the unique valid solution.
The alternative bypass line equation admits exactly one real solution within its operational domain.
Squaring both sides of the isolated radical equation $\sqrt{2x+7} = x+2$ produces the candidate roots $x = -3$ and $x = 1$, of which $x = -3$ is an extraneous root.
The directional regulator valve equation $|3x - 2| = 2x - 5$ admits two distinct real solutions whose sum is strictly positive.
Substituting $u = x^2 - 2x$ into the harmonic booster pump cycle equation generates two quadratic equations in $x$, yielding a total of four distinct real solutions whose sum equals 4.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

To solve a rational equation, one must first identify domain restrictions where denominators equal zero and then check for extraneous solutions created by clearing fractions.

The factorized denominators of the main return line equation are $x-1$, $x+2$, and $(x-1)(x+2)$. The domain restriction is:

$$x \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{-2, 1\}$$

Clearing denominators leads to:

$$x^2 - 1 = 0$$

$$
x = 1 \quad \text{or} \quad x = -1
$$

Because $x = 1$ makes the denominator $x-1$ zero, it is an extraneous root and must be rejected. The only admissible solution is $x = -1$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

A solution to a rational equation is admissible only if it belongs to the domain of all rational expressions in the original equation.

For the bypass line equation, the denominators are $x-3$, $x+3$, and $x^2 - 9$. The domain restriction is:

$$x \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{-3, 3\}$$

Clearing the common denominator $x^2 - 9$ yields:

$$x^2 + x + 6 = x^2 + 9$$

$$x = 3$$

The only algebraic candidate is $x = 3$, which makes the denominators $x-3$ and $x^2-9$ zero. Consequently, $x = 3$ is extraneous, and the equation has zero real solutions in its operational domain.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Squaring both sides of a radical equation is not an equivalence transformation and can introduce extraneous roots where the non-radical side was negative.

Isolating the radical gives $\sqrt{2x+7} = x+2$. Squaring both sides yields:

$$2x + 7 = (x+2)^2$$

$$2x + 7 = x^2 + 4x + 4$$

$$x^2 + 2x - 3 = 0$$

$$(x+3)(x-1) = 0$$

The algebraic candidates are $x = -3$ and $x = 1$. Substituting $x = -3$ into the isolated equation gives:

$$
\sqrt{2(-3)+7} = \sqrt{1} = 1 \neq -3 + 2 = -1
$$

Substituting $x = 1$ gives:

$$
\sqrt{2(1)+7} = \sqrt{9} = 3 = 1 + 2
$$

Thus $x = -3$ is extraneous while $x = 1$ is valid.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

An equation of the form $|A| = B$ requires $B \ge 0$ and splits into the two cases $A = B$ and $A = -B$.

For $|3x - 2| = 2x - 5$, the right-hand side requires:

$$2x - 5 \ge 0 \iff x \ge \frac{5}{2}$$

Analyzing the first case where $3x - 2 \ge 0$ gives:

$$
3x - 2 = 2x - 5 \iff x = -3
$$

This candidate contradicts $x \ge \frac{5}{2}$. Analyzing the second case where $3x - 2 < 0$ gives:

$$
-(3x - 2) = 2x - 5 \iff 5x = 7 \iff x = \frac{7}{5}
$$

This candidate also contradicts $x \ge \frac{5}{2}$. The equation has no real solutions.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

An equation of degree four containing terms of the form $(g(x))^2$ and $g(x)$ can be solved by setting $u = g(x)$.

Letting $u = x^2 - 2x$ transforms the equation into:

$$u^2 - 11u + 24 = 0$$

$$(u-3)(u-8) = 0$$

This yields two intermediate values, $u = 3$ and $u = 8$. For $u = 3$, we solve:

$$
x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0 \iff (x-3)(x+1) = 0 \iff x \in \{-1, 3\}
$$

For $u = 8$, we solve:

$$
x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0 \iff (x-4)(x+2) = 0 \iff x \in \{-2, 4\}
$$

The four distinct real solutions are $-2, -1, 3, 4$. Their sum is:

$$
(-2) + (-1) + 3 + 4 = 4
$$

This matches the claim.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
The five flow-rate equations describe distinct algebraic structures across rational, radical, absolute-value, and quadratic-substitution models.

For the main return line, factoring the denominator gives $x^2 + x - 2 = (x-1)(x+2)$, which establishes the domain $D_1 = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{-2, 1\}$. Multiplying both sides by the common denominator $(x-1)(x+2)$ yields:

$$2x(x+2) - 3(x-1) = 6 + (x-1)(x+2)$$

$$2x^2 + x + 3 = x^2 + x + 4$$

$$x^2 - 1 = 0$$

For the alternative bypass line, the common denominator is $(x-3)(x+3) = x^2 - 9$, imposing the domain $D_2 = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{-3, 3\}$. Multiplying through by $x^2 - 9$ produces:

$$x(x+3) - 2(x-3) = 18 + (x^2 - 9)$$

$$x^2 + x + 6 = x^2 + 9$$

$$x = 3$$

For the suction line, isolating the radical gives $\sqrt{2x+7} = x+2$. Squaring both sides under the requirement $x+2 \ge 0$ leads to:

$$2x + 7 = x^2 + 4x + 4$$

$$x^2 + 2x - 3 = 0$$

For the regulator valve, the absolute-value equation $|3x-2| = 2x-5$ requires $2x - 5 \ge 0$ because the absolute value cannot be negative.

For the booster pump, the substitution $u = x^2 - 2x$ transforms the fourth-degree polynomial into a quadratic in $u$:

$$u^2 - 11u + 24 = 0$$

$$1\cdot 18 = 18$$

$$y = \frac{-74}{-2}$$

math.title: Meetings, vertex, and a rewrite in $f$
math.context: Let $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}-4x+1$. Work in symbols; no figure is supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The sum of the meeting abscissas of the two graphs equals $5$.
The axis of $g$ is $x=2$, which is half the Vieta sum of the roots of $g$.
The vertex of $g$ lies $3$ units below the horizontal axis.
The product of the roots of $g$ equals $1$, matching $g(0)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Meetings of a line and a parabola are the real zeros of their difference. Subtract the given line from the given parabola.

$$g(x)-f(x)=(x^{2}-4x+1)-(x+1)$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-5x$$

The difference factors at sight, so the two abscissas are $0$ and $5$. Vieta already reads their sum from the middle coefficient.

$$
x(x-5)=0,\qquad 0+5 = 5
$$

A quadratic difference has at most two real zeros, and both of them appear here, adding to $5$.

The sum of the meeting abscissas is $5$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The axis of $ax^{2}+bx+c$ is the vertical line through $-b/(2a)$, and it ignores the constant term entirely.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4x+1$$

$$x=-\frac{-4}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=-\frac{-4}{2}$$

$$x=2$$

Vieta's sum of the roots is $-b/a=4$, and half of that sum is the same abscissa.

$$\frac{4}{2}$$

$$g(x)=2$$

The constant term $1$ never enters the axis formula, which is why $x=2$ can be read off $a$ and $b$ alone.

$$S=-b/a$$

$$S=4$$

$$x=S/2$$

$$x=2$$

The axis is $x=2$, which is half the Vieta sum of the roots of $g$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The vertex height is the value of $g$ on its axis $x=2$. Substitute that abscissa term by term.

$$g(2)=4-8+1$$

$$g(2)=4-8$$

$$g(2)=-4$$

$$g(2)=-4+1$$

$$g(2)=-3$$

A point of height $-3$ sits three units below the horizontal axis. Completing the square makes the same height visible as the constant beside the square.

$$g(x)=(x-2)^{2}-3$$

A negative vertex height for an upward parabola means the graph dips below the axis between its two real roots.

$$-3<0$$

The vertex lies $3$ units below the axis.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Vieta reads the product of the roots from the constant term over the leading coefficient, without solving.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4x+1$$

$$P=\frac{c}{a}$$

$$P=1$$

The same number is $g(0)$, because every term with an $x$ dies at the origin.

$$g(0)=1$$

The identity

$$P=c/a$$

$$P=g(0)$$

 holds for every monic quadratic, because only the constant term survives at the origin.

$$g(0)=1$$

$$g(0)=P$$

The product of the roots is $1$, matching $g(0)$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Because $f$ is a non-constant line, the square $f(x)^{2}$ already carries an $x^{2}$ term, so $1$, $f$ and $f^{2}$ span every parabola. Expand the claimed combination.

$$f(x)^{2}=(x+1)^{2}$$

$$f(x)^{2}=x^{2}+2x+1$$

$$f(x)^{2}-6f(x)+6=x^{2}+2x+1-6(x+1)+6$$

$$f(x)^{2}-6f(x)+6=x^{2}-4x+1$$

Matching coefficients of $x^{2}$, then $x$, then the constant term, is always possible once $f$ is a non-constant line.

$$g(x)=f(x)^{2}-6f(x)+6$$

The combination reproduces $g$ identically, so the claimed rewrite holds.

So the statement is True.
math.solution_overview:
Both rules are handed over with numbers already in place.

$$
f(x) = 2x+1,\qquad g(x) = x^{2}-3x+1
$$

The turning point of $g$ is worth having in hand: the axis comes from the first two coefficients, and evaluating $g$ there supplies the height.

$$
x = \frac{3}{2},\qquad g\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) = -\frac{5}{4}
$$

$$
g(x) = \left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{5}{4},\qquad \mathrm{ver} = \left(\frac{3}{2},-\frac{5}{4}\right)
$$

Coefficients alone settle the sum and the product of the roots of $g$, and the discriminant tells how many of those roots are real.

$$
S = 3,\qquad P = 1,\qquad \Delta_{g} = 5
$$

Wherever the two graphs touch, the difference $g-f$ is zero; that difference is quadratic and its discriminant leaves two crossings.

$$
g(x)-f(x) = x^{2}-5x,\qquad \Delta = 25
$$

$$
x = 0,\qquad x = 5
$$

Because $f$ is a line with non-zero slope, the square $f(x)^{2}$ already carries an $x^{2}$ term, so $g$ can be rebuilt from $f(x)^{2}$, $f(x)$ and a constant. Matching coefficients gives the triple named in letter E.

$$
